clue.text: Widely admired tree round university

indicators.note: one thing placed round another encloses it, so the tree wraps the university

explanation.surface: A much-loved tree that grows around a university campus.
explanation.definitionFit: Something popular is liked by many people, so it is widely admired.

clue.text: Prediction of support by ambassador on Cyprus

parts.note: HE, His Excellency, is the title of an ambassador
CY is the international code for Cyprus

explanation.surface: A forecast that an ambassador will back Cyprus.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the first two pieces sit on top of the last.
explanation.definitionFit: A prophecy is a foretelling of the future, which is a prediction.

clue.text: Free ticket left with travel document

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A complimentary ticket handed over with someone's travel papers.
explanation.definitionFit: A passport is the official document a traveller shows when crossing borders.

clue.text: Ring up about one flowering shrub

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards
about means surrounding, so the word goes round the next piece

parts.note: to ring someone is to call them

explanation.surface: Phoning someone to ask about a single flowering bush.
explanation.definitionFit: Lilac is a garden shrub with fragrant purple or white flower clusters.

clue.text: Reference book — author gets users confused

indicators.note: confused means jumbled up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A writer's readers are left baffled by a reference work.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is neatly apt: a thesaurus is the classic book an author consults.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Mark Roget's thesaurus is the famous English book of synonyms, a standard reference work.

clue.text: Wear out short military overalls

indicators.note: something short is missing its end, so the last letter is cut off

explanation.surface: A soldier's cut-down combat overalls getting worn through.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, fatigue means to tire someone out, a synonym of wear out.

clue.text: The current chefs working in a London station

indicators.note: working suggests being set in motion and moved about, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Today's cooks are employed at a London railway terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: Fenchurch Street is a London railway terminus in the City, serving Essex; it is also a Monopoly square.
explanation.definitionFit: Fenchurch Street is one of London's mainline railway stations.

clue.text: Goes across with dramatist touring south-east

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the dramatist's name goes round the next piece

parts.note: Ben Travers wrote the Aldwych farces

explanation.surface: A playwright on a tour of England's south-east.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Travers was an English writer of 1920s farces such as Rookery Nook, a crossword favourite for 'dramatist'.
explanation.definitionFit: To traverse a place is to travel across it, so traverses means goes across.

clue.text: Mineral used to make good long weapon

parts.note: a lance is a long spear used by cavalry

explanation.surface: A mineral employed to forge a fine long weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: Glance is a fairly obscure word for a lustrous metallic ore, as in lead glance.
explanation.definitionFit: In mining, glance names various ores with a metallic shine, such as galena, so it is a mineral.

clue.text: Small opening I, reportedly, must have allowed

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said, so the pronoun is taken by its sound

parts.note: the pronoun sounds the same as the organ of sight

explanation.surface: Someone insisting they must have permitted a small gap.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyelet is a small hole, often metal-rimmed, for a lace or cord to pass through.

clue.text: Bird in farmhouse larder

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A bird has got into the pantry of a farmhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: The ousel, or ouzel, is an old name for the blackbird and related thrushes.

clue.text: George, with trendy friend, meeting one in gaudy bar

parts.note: G is a common abbreviation for George
an ace counts as one on dice and cards

explanation.surface: George and his fashionable mate meet someone in a flashy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A gin palace was a showily decorated Victorian pub; the term is now used for any over-ornate bar or flashy yacht.
explanation.definitionFit: Gin palaces were famous for their glittering mirrors and gilt, the very picture of a garish drinking place.

clue.text: What's bound to put an end to children's game?

parts.note: a bound is a jump, i.e. a hop
to scotch a rumour or plan is to stop it

explanation.surface: A riddle asking what is certain to stop children playing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' reads as 'certain to', but bound is a noun here, a leap.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopscotch is the playground game of hopping through chalked squares.

clue.text: Military decoration, we hear, for a compere

indicators.note: what we hear is the sound of the letters, so the abbreviation is spoken rather than written

parts.note: the MC, or Military Cross, is a British gallantry award, and its letters are spoken

explanation.surface: A medal is awarded to a host, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: EMCEE spells out how M.C., master of ceremonies, is said.
explanation.definitionFit: An emcee is a master of ceremonies, the host who introduces acts, which is what a compere does.

clue.text: Low, perhaps, a US art critic abroad

indicators.note: abroad suggests being scattered far from home, so the letters are dispersed and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, every letter used

explanation.surface: An American art critic travelling overseas is feeling down.
explanation.walkthrough: Low looks like an adjective for mood; it is David Low, the New Zealand-born cartoonist famous for his political cartoons in London newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: David Low was a celebrated political cartoonist, an example of someone who draws exaggerated portraits.

clue.text: All the customers tell niece off

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: All the shoppers scold a young relative.
explanation.definitionFit: A clientele is a business's whole body of customers.

clue.text: Titled lady one's seen in pubs

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the first piece is set within the drinking places

explanation.surface: A noblewoman who is spotted in public houses.
explanation.definitionFit: A baroness holds the rank of baron's wife or a peerage in her own right, so she is a titled lady.

clue.text: Play safe and bowl

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
a pan is a bowl-shaped vessel

explanation.surface: A cricket instruction: play safely and bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: Play, safe and bowl all suggest cricket; peter for a safe is old underworld slang, hence safecrackers being 'peter men'.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Pan is J. M. Barrie's famous stage play about the boy who never grows up.

clue.text: Elephant seal, twice floundering, has to make a fresh start

indicators.note: floundering means struggling clumsily, so the letters thrash about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; twice is part of the fodder, not a doubling instruction

explanation.surface: A struggling elephant seal, having floundered twice, must start over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' looks like it modifies floundering, but its letters belong in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to forget past mistakes and begin again, as if erasing a written slate.

clue.text: Bushwhacker injured chest round end of July

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the mixed letters go round the selected one
something injured is knocked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged
end of picks out only the final letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A jungle explorer has hurt their chest by the end of July.
explanation.walkthrough: Bushwhacker suggests a person; here it is a tool that whacks bushes.
explanation.definitionFit: A scythe cuts down long grass and undergrowth, so it is literally something that whacks at bushes.

clue.text: Come together in side at college

parts.note: a student at university is said to be up, especially at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: Joining forces in a college team.
explanation.definitionFit: To team up is to join with others to work together, which is to come together.

clue.text: See 17
Take choir out for a kind of tea that may be served in Hanoi

definitions.text: a kind of tea that may be served in Hanoi

indicators.note: out suggests being put out of order or out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Taking a choir out for tea while touring Vietnam.
explanation.walkthrough: Artichoke tea, made from the dried plant, is a popular drink in Vietnam, especially around Da Lat.
explanation.definitionFit: Vietnamese herbal infusions include one brewed from artichoke leaves and flowers, so the vegetable names a type of tea.

clue.text: Class actors close to home

parts.note: the cast is the set of actors in a production

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is kept

explanation.surface: A class of drama students live near home.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a hereditary social class, particularly in the Hindu system.

clue.text: Widdicombe Fair chap pointing to fruit in book

indicators.note: one thing in another is enclosed by it, so the fruit goes inside the book

parts.note: a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: A character from a folk song points to some fruit in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Widdicombe Fair is an English folk song from Devon whose refrain begins 'Tom Pearse, Tom Pearse, lend me your grey mare'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Pearse is the owner of the grey mare in the Devon folk song, so he is the song's chap.

clue.text: Brush stroke

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to clean with a broom
second meaning: a long swinging movement, as of an oar or arm

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brush stroke' reads as a painter's mark; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to clean with a broom and a broad swinging movement of the arm or a bat.

clue.text: Reveal former printing machine

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
a press prints books and papers

explanation.surface: Unveiling an old printing press.
explanation.definitionFit: To express feelings is to make them known, so it is a synonym of reveal.

clue.text: Senator solved crime

indicators.note: a solved puzzle has been worked out, so these letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A politician has cracked a criminal case.
explanation.definitionFit: Treason, betraying one's country, is a serious criminal offence.
